analysis.one_liner: Requires coal power plants to install the strictest controls on mercury emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut mercury emissions from coal power plants never left committee; it was introduced with only two cosponsors and received no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to require the EPA to set the strictest achievable control technology standards for mercury emissions from coal-fired power plants. Power plants are the leading source of airborne mercury, a neurotoxin that accumulates in fish and poses risks to pregnant women and children. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Environment Subcommittee, where it remained without action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live downwind of coal plants and anyone who eats fish caught in U.S. waters, especially women of child-bearing age and developing children, would gain from reduced mercury exposure; the bill's findings note 44 states had mercury fish consumption advisories.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fish consumers, especially pregnant women and children

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to set Maximum Achievable Control Technology (MACT) standards for mercury emissions from electric utility steam generating units, the same standard applied to all other major mercury sources under Clean Air Act section 112.
The bill's findings state that coal-fired power plants are the leading source of U.S. air emissions of mercury, a potent neurotoxin that can cause adverse health effects at very low concentrations.
The findings cite about 3,852 fish consumption advisories across 48 states and note that 44 states have issued advisories due to mercury, showing the breadth of public exposure.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-fired electric utilities, which would have to install and operate maximum achievable control technology to cut mercury emissions; costs would likely be passed to electricity customers in coal-reliant regions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal power plants and their customers

drawbacks.text: Requiring the strictest available control technology on every coal unit imposes significant compliance and capital costs on coal-fired utilities, which would likely be recovered through higher electricity prices, falling hardest in regions dependent on coal power.

The bill mandates a specific regulatory path by statute rather than leaving the standard-setting process to the EPA, which removes agency flexibility in weighing costs and technological feasibility for individual plants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefits of cutting mercury, a neurotoxin linked to developmental harm in children, are broad and long-lasting, while the costs fall on a concentrated industry and spread thinly across electricity customers. A good-faith objection is that a statutory MACT mandate raises power costs with less flexibility than EPA-set rules, but the bill addresses a health hazard the record shows is widespread.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Environment Subcommittee, and no further action ever happened.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 3, 2009 by Rep. Eddie Bernice Johnson with Rep. Grijalva as an original cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment, where it stalled.
The bill ended the 111th Congress without a committee vote, a floor vote, or any further action, with only two cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired electric utilities avoided a mandate to install the strictest mercury controls, and electricity customers in coal-reliant areas avoided potential price increases. Communities near coal plants and fish consumers gained nothing, since mercury emissions stayed on the regulatory status quo.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were House Democrats, but no one actively opposed it in the record; it simply died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would require them to install maximum achievable control technology to cut mercury emissions, the standard applied to every other major mercury source under the Clean Air Act. Their interest in avoiding those costs ran against the public's interest in reducing a neurotoxin from the leading industrial source.
Stricter emissions controls could raise the cost of burning coal and accelerate plant retirements, reducing coal demand; the bill does not regulate mining directly.
